title: Reading and answering scenario questions
summary: A scenario card gives a few fixed constraints and hides the rest. You choose an option, then check its verdict, reason and trade-off against the constraints.
useIf: You practise with scenario cards and want to learn from the verdicts, not only collect a score.
avoidIf: You want a single memorised answer per card. Verdicts change when the dials change.

explain.md: Every scenario card has the same parts. The **situation** gives facts, and facts it gives are real. The **constraints** list the dial values that are fixed in this card. The **unknowns** are questions a strong candidate would ask, and they mark dials you must not assume. The **options** each carry a verdict, a reason and a trade-off. After you choose, you see all of them, plus the **flips**: changed constraints that would change the winner.

steps.title: Read the unknowns
steps.md: Do not assume them. Note which could change your pick.

steps.title: Cross out
steps.md: Drop options that break a stated constraint.

steps.title: Pick by cost of error
steps.md: Among the rest, choose the one that is cheapest to be wrong about.

steps.title: Check the flips
steps.md: Ask what you would change if one flip happened.

explain.md: The card is **answerable from the stated constraints**. If you need a fact it does not give, that fact is an unknown, and the right move is to say how the answer would change, not to invent a value. Choose in two passes. First eliminate: an option that breaks a stated constraint is out, whatever its reputation. Then compare the survivors by the cost of being wrong, including how hard each is to reverse. Write one sentence of reasoning before you reveal, because the reveal is only useful if you can compare it with your own logic.

explain.caption: What the verdicts mean
head: Verdict
Meaning
How to use it when revising
rows: best
Fits every stated constraint at an acceptable cost. Exactly one per card.
Learn the constraint that made it win and its stated trade-off.
good
Acceptable, with a cost the best option avoids.
Know the cost, because a flip can promote it to best.
poor
Fails a stated constraint or adds cost the constraints do not need.
Read where it would be right, because it is usually best somewhere else.

explain.title: Poor options are not wrong options
explain.md: Every poor option explains the situation where it would win. Revise those sentences: they are your flip conditions for the interview.

whereToUse: Every topic page in this guide ends with scenario cards that follow this format
Group sessions, where pairs commit to an option before the reveal
Self-testing: write your reason first, then compare it with the card's reason
Interview practice: turn the card's constraints into the clarifying questions you would ask

use: You can name the constraint that rules out at least one option
You want to practise trade-off language such as 'this costs us X'
You review a topic and need a quick test of whether you understood the dials
avoid: You are guessing: a lucky pick teaches nothing, so write your reason before you reveal
You carry a favourite tool into every card: the card tests the constraints, not the tool
You only want the score: the value sits in the reasons and the flips, which the score hides
flips: You consistently pick the sophisticated option: re-read the cost column of each card
You always pick the cheap one: look for the constraint, such as per-user permissions, that rules it out
A card feels unanswerable: read the unknowns, they list what the card deliberately leaves open

pitfalls.symptom: You choose an option and then explain why the card is wrong
pitfalls.cause: You added an assumption the card did not state
pitfalls.fix: Reread the constraints and the unknowns, and treat unstated facts as open questions

pitfalls.symptom: You treat 'good' as a wrong answer
pitfalls.cause: You read verdicts as a score instead of a cost statement
pitfalls.fix: Read the trade-off of the good option: it names the cost, and a flip can make it the best

pitfalls.symptom: You pick the most advanced option every time
pitfalls.fix: Check whether a stated constraint needs it, and prefer the cheapest option that meets every constraint

scenarios.title: Small stable corpus, tight latency
scenarios.situation: A team needs an assistant over about 150,000 tokens of documentation. Answers must arrive within 3 seconds at p95.
unknowns: How much accuracy drops deep inside a long prompt on this model?
How many questions per day reuse the same prefix?
scenarios.question: Which option fits the stated constraints?

options.name: RAG with hybrid search
options.tradeoff: Adds ingestion, an index and retrieval tuning for a corpus that fits the window.

options.name: Fine-tune a model on the documentation
options.why: Studies found retrieval beats fine-tuning for injecting knowledge [[r27]].
options.tradeoff: Fine-tuning is right for tone, format or a smaller model, not for facts.

options.name: Put the documents in the prompt and use prompt caching
options.why: The corpus is under the roughly 200,000 token level Anthropic suggests can go straight into a prompt [[r26]], it is stable, and a cached prefix keeps latency and cost down.
options.tradeoff: Accuracy can fall for facts buried deep in a long input, so test with a golden set at different depths.

flips.if: The corpus grows to several million tokens
flips.then: RAG wins, because the corpus no longer fits.

flips.if: Each user may see only some documents

scenarios.takeaway: Constraints rule options out, then cost picks among the rest.

scenarios.title: Two options fit every constraint
scenarios.situation: On a card, two options both satisfy every stated constraint. One is simpler and easy to reverse. The other is more capable but needs new infrastructure.
constraints: Both options meet the stated dials
unknowns: Which unstated dial would favour the more capable option?
scenarios.question: How do you choose and justify?

options.name: Ask for more information and decide after the answer
options.tradeoff: On a card or with a time limit you must still commit and state your assumption.

options.name: Choose the simpler, reversible option, and name the unknown that would flip you
options.why: Cost of being wrong is lowest, and naming the flip shows you know when the other option wins.
options.tradeoff: If the flip happens you will migrate later.

options.name: Choose the more capable option because it covers more cases
options.why: It adds infrastructure that no stated constraint needs.
options.tradeoff: It is right once an unstated dial, such as rapid growth, is confirmed.

flips.if: Requirements are fixed and the capable option has a known payoff
The team has already run the infrastructure for other products
flips.then: The cost gap narrows and the capable option can win.

scenarios.takeaway: When two fit, take the cheaper to reverse and name the flip.

quiz.q: What does a 'good' verdict mean on a scenario card?
options: The option is wrong but close
The option is the best in another situation
The option scores half a point
The option is acceptable, with a cost the best option avoids
quiz.explain: Good means acceptable with a cost. A poor option is the one that fails a constraint and states where it would be right. Verdicts are not scores.

quiz.q: Order the steps for reading a card.
items: Read the unknowns without assuming them
Cross out options that break a constraint
Pick the cheapest option to be wrong about
quiz.explain: Constraints come first because they eliminate options. Cost of error decides among the survivors, and the flips test your pick.

quiz.q: Which habits make you misread scenario cards?
options: Adding facts the card did not state
Choosing the most sophisticated option by default
Writing your reason before the reveal
quiz.explain: Assumptions, a bias toward sophistication and skipping the unknowns all cause misreads. Writing your reason first is the habit that fixes them.

flashcards.front: What do the constraints on a scenario card tell you?
flashcards.back: Which dials are fixed in this card. Facts not listed are open, and the unknowns name the questions you would ask.

flashcards.front: How do you use a poor option when revising?
flashcards.back: Read where it would be right. That sentence is a flip condition you can say in an interview.

flashcards.front: Two options both fit every constraint. What do you do?
flashcards.back: Pick the cheaper one to reverse and name the unknown that would flip you to the other.
